newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Weary Mobutu back in Zaire, U.S. troops head out.
newsitem.headline: Weary Mobutu back in Zaire, U.S. troops head out.

text.p: Ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, his popularity plummeting, was back in Zaire on Saturday to try to salvage what remains of his crumbling authority in the face of relentless rebel advances.
The United States said on Friday it was sending hundreds of troops to West Africa to prepare for a possible evacuation of Americans from Zaire.
The U.S. forces would join French troops and planes already in nearby Gabon and Congo in case evacuations from Zaire became necessary.

"The Department of Defence has directed the U.S. European Command to deploy enabling forces, consisting of several hundred personnel, as part of contingency planning for a possible future evacuation from Zaire," the Pentagon said in a statement.

Mobutu's low-key homecoming on Friday, a far cry from the enthusiastic welcome he received on December 17, contrasted sharply with rebel leader Laurent Kabila's triumphant entry into Zaire's third city of Kisangani earlier in the day.

Exhausted by fresh cancer treatment and a difficult flight home from France, Mobutu sent away a high-ranking welcoming committee and the world's press -- apparently anxious not to be seen being helped down the aircraft steps.
"It was a difficult flight," one close aide told Reuters, adding that Mobutu was resting at his official residence.
France and the United States were both monitoring events for signs of any need to airlift out their nationals.

Mobutu, 66, has spent most of his time in Europe since having prostate cancer surgery in August. He has dominated Zaire with a mixture of political acumen and military ruthlessness since seizing power in 1965.

He left hospital in Monaco on Wednesday after fresh cancer treatment. He issued a statement on Thursday calling for a truce and for a national council to find ways out of the crisis "with all our brothers, without exclusion".
France, his last international backer, hailed his call.
"For us his intentions seem unambiguous and are consistent with the essential aims of the peace process," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told reporters in Paris.
But Kabila, whose rebels have been fighting to topple Mobutu since October, was unimpressed. He rejected Mobutu's truce-then-talks call, saying: "We negotiate first."
More than 10,000 jubilant residents turned out in Kisangani, which fell to the rebels last weekend, to welcome Kabila as a saviour.

On December 17, tens of thousands of people turned out in Kinshasa to welcome Mobutu back from Europe. On Friday small groups gathered in opposition areas along the route to the airport to jeer him and praise Kabila.
The president's son Mobutu Nzanga said in France his father planned to address the nation. "My father remains an important player in the stability of Central Africa," he added.

He said his father no longer ruled out talks with rebel leaders but wanted to involve the government, army and transitional parliament. "His intention is to find a solution to the present crisis in consultation with parliament, the government and the military high command."
But many ordinary Zaireans, eager for a change from poverty and hardship under Mobutu, are openly rallying to Kabila.

His Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) has been advancing relentlessly across the sprawling and chaotic nation, where central government control has long been notional in many places.
Although under foreign pressure to agree a truce and talk, Kabila says only face-to-face talks with Mobutu can halt the fighting.
